response:
Diagnosis: the archive has now cleanly split. Signals whose valuation leg is a conventional equity yield (GP/P, B/P, E/P, financing-mix, earned-capital-per-share) reliably produce large Fama-MacBeth t-stats (4–5.7) but zero-to-negative FF5 alpha — HML/RMW own that spread. Everything with a *liquid balance-sheet* leg produces positive alpha: net-cash cheapness × gross profit (+2.7%, t=2.65), net-cash cheapness × liability coverage (+3.7%, t=2.64, Sharpe 0.24, but coverage only 0.091), and B/M × asset liquidity (+1.9%, t=1.96, Sharpe 0.29, fmb 4.19). The unexploited alpha therefore lives in how liquid and unencumbered the claim behind the discount is, not in the discount itself. This generation consolidates that axis (S1–S3), repairs the coverage loss of the best alpha (S1), tests whether asset liquidity works through safety or through productivity (S5), and fixes the persistent sign conflict on the short side (S6).

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Net Cash Cheapness With Accrual-Free Coverage
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), lt), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: Cash-rich cheapness is rewarded when the operating business also throws off enough cash earnings to service the obligations it does carry; measuring that coverage with income-statement cash earnings rather than the cash-flow statement keeps the same economics while extending the measurable sample.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The archive's highest alpha came from exactly this mechanism but at coverage 0.091, roughly a third below its siblings, because reported operating cash flow is unavailable for large parts of the panel; substituting ib+dp restores the sample without changing the economic content of coverage. If alpha and t-statistic hold up on the wider sample, the balance-sheet-safety channel is confirmed as robust rather than a small-sample artifact.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Net Cash Cheapness With Dual Quality Screen
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), RATIO(act, at))))
HYPOTHESIS: Profitability and asset liquidity are distinct guarantees behind a discounted price — one says the business earns, the other says the assets are convertible — and a cheap, cash-rich firm that offers both is much less likely to be a trap than one offering either alone.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Both quality channels have independently produced positive FF5 alpha against different valuation legs, so combining them into a single ranked quality composite tests whether their information is additive or redundant. Using SUMRANK inside one industry rank avoids compounding two multiplicative shrinkages, which would otherwise concentrate the long leg in an unstably small corner of the cross-section.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Net Liquid Claim Cheapness With Gross Profit
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: The shareholder's hard claim is current assets less every liability — receivables, inventory and cash that could in principle be realised against obligations — and a firm priced low relative to that net liquid claim while still earning gross profit is mispriced rather than distressed.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: This upgrades the valuation leg from cash-versus-financial-debt to the full Graham net-current-asset claim, which unlike the earlier flagged che-minus-lt construction is genuinely two-sided in the cross-section because current assets are of comparable magnitude to total liabilities for most firms. Holding the profitability leg fixed against the archive's net-cash version isolates whether the alpha comes from cash specifically or from any unencumbered liquid claim.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Enterprise Price Per Dollar Of Gross Profit
EXPRESSION: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(MUL(prcc_f, csho), che), ADD(dltt, dlc)), MA(SUB(revt, cogs), 3)), 1)
HYPOTHESIS: The relevant expensiveness is what an acquirer pays for the operating business after cash is removed and debt added, measured per dollar of durable gross profit; firms with a high enterprise price per unit of profit are overvalued regardless of how their equity multiples look and should underperform.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Expressing the idea as a multiple with a negative expected sign, rather than as a yield, means the pathological cases work in favour of the economics: deep net-cash firms with negative enterprise value land at the most negative extreme, which under a negative expected sign is the highest-return tail where the stub-value story places them. Three-year averaged gross profit keeps the denominator positive and stable for essentially all firms, and the construct separates operating-business valuation from the balance-sheet cash that the archive's positive-alpha family rewards.
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Cheapness Backed By Working Liquid Assets
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(revt, act)))
HYPOTHESIS: Liquid assets support a low valuation only when they are actually turning: receivables that get collected and inventory that sells are convertible value, while a large current-asset balance that generates little revenue is stale inventory and uncollectible receivables that will be written down.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The archive shows B/M times the *level* of asset liquidity earns positive alpha, but level cannot distinguish convertible working assets from accumulating dead ones; replacing the level with current-asset turnover tests directly which interpretation drives the result. The pair of signals is jointly diagnostic — if turnover works better, the mechanism is realisability of book value, if the level works better, it is balance-sheet safety.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Rich Price On A Strained Balance Sheet
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(lt, act)))
HYPOTHESIS: The most reliably overpriced firms are those whose market value already embeds optimistic growth while their obligations tower over their liquid resources; when expectations disappoint, these firms must recapitalise from a position of weakness, so richly priced and illiquid balance sheets should earn low returns.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Both prior short-side attempts carried a high-book-to-market or liabilities-to-price leg whose unconditional cross-sectional slope is positive, which fought the negative expected sign and produced wrong-signed Fama-MacBeth t-stats despite correct-signed alphas; orienting the valuation leg toward expensiveness aligns both statistics on the same side. The quality leg, total liabilities relative to current assets, is a stock-based strain measure rather than a flow measure, so it identifies firms that cannot cover claims from realisable assets even if current earnings look adequate.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---CRITIQUE Net Cash Cheapness With Accrual-Free Coverage---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is a one-input substitution (oancf → ib+dp) in an archived signal with identical economics and identical structure — a cosmetic coverage-driven variant rather than a substantively different mechanism, and the accrual-vs-cash distinction it discards is precisely the earnings-quality content the archive's other signals treat as informative.

---CRITIQUE Net Cash Cheapness With Dual Quality Screen---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: Internally consistent and thoughtfully constructed (SUMRANK avoids double multiplicative shrinkage), but it is an incremental blend of two already-tested legs whose quality inputs are likely correlated, so the additivity test is worth running yet unlikely to be a large step forward.

---CRITIQUE Net Liquid Claim Cheapness With Gross Profit---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The valuation leg is essentially Graham's net-current-asset-value, a long-documented anomaly, but gating it on averaged gross profitability and contrasting it directly against the archived net-cash version is a legitimate and well-specified discrimination test rather than a plain rediscovery.

---CRITIQUE Enterprise Price Per Dollar Of Gross Profit---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is a direct rediscovery of the published enterprise-multiple anomaly (Loughran–Wellman), and the negative-EV rationale is shaky because the signal is non-monotone in cheapness — near-zero-EV firms rank mid-sample while the extreme long tail is populated by the sparse negative-EV cases the construct is being justified by.

---CRITIQUE Cheapness Backed By Working Liquid Assets---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: A coherent and genuinely diagnostic contrast to the archived B/M × current-asset-level signal, though revt/act is close to standard asset-turnover quality (an F-score ingredient) and is mechanically negatively related to act/at, so a result could partly just invert the earlier finding rather than explain it.

---CRITIQUE Rich Price On A Strained Balance Sheet---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The sign diagnosis of prior short-side failures is the most intelligent reasoning in this batch and the expression's direction matches the stated hypothesis, but the glamour-plus-leverage combination is close to the documented distress/leverage-with-growth effect, and multiplying two [0,1] ranks leaves the long (low-value) leg an uninterpretable mix of cheap-and-strained with expensive-and-unstrained firms.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Net Cash Cheapness With Accrual Conservatism
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, lct), 1), dp), at))))
HYPOTHESIS: A cash-rich, low-debt firm trading at a discount is mispriced when its reported profits are not being manufactured by working-capital build-up; if the same balance-sheet cheapness comes with heavy accruals, the cash position is a snapshot that operating reversals will erode.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: Instead of substituting a proxy inside an archived signal, this pairs the valuation leg that has generated every positive FF5 alpha in the archive with the one quality dimension the archive has never combined with it — the accrual-versus-cash content of earnings — which is orthogonal to RMW and absent from FF5 altogether. The accrual measure is built from balance-sheet primitives (act, lct, dp) so it does not inherit the sample restriction of the cash-flow statement, keeping coverage close to the 0.14 tier rather than the 0.09 tier.
REASONING_END

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Cheapness With A Written-Down Asset Base
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(dp, 5), at)))
HYPOTHESIS: Historical-cost accounting understates the value of an old, heavily depreciated asset base, so a firm that is cheap on book value while having charged five years of depreciation large relative to its current assets is cheap against an understated denominator; a firm equally cheap with a freshly capitalised asset base has no such hidden margin.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: This replaces the enterprise-multiple rediscovery with an accounting-conservatism channel: cumulative depreciation relative to the current asset base is an asset-vintage state, monotone and non-negative for every firm, so there is no sign discontinuity or sparse-tail dependence. The mechanism explains why some low price-to-book firms are genuinely cheap — their book denominator is stale — which is a quality-of-book story rather than a quality-of-earnings story and is not represented in HML, RMW or CMA.
REASONING_END
